## The goal

On January 7, 2025, two wildfires ignited in Los Angeles County,
California: the Palisades fire and the Eaton fire. This homework asks a
plain question about that event: how bad did the air get, at one
monitor, in downtown Los Angeles?

You answer with six numbers: the highest daily reading of that winter,
the day it happened, the January 2025 average, the number of days above
the health standard, the number of days with no reading at all, and the
peak relative to the December average.

The data is from the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the
federal environmental regulator. It reports PM2.5: airborne particles
smaller than 2.5 micrometers, the standard measure of smoke, in
micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³). EPA's 24-hour health standard is
35 µg/m³.

Everything is base R: `read.csv()`, subsetting, dates, `NA`. No
packages.

The files come to you exactly as EPA ships them. `read.csv()` silently
damages two of the columns. The winter window has more days than the
file has rows, and the gaps carry no marker. Working from the file as
shipped, and catching what it does to you, is the assignment.

## The data

EPA AirData publishes a daily summary from every regulatory air
monitor in the United States. Your two files cover one site: 060371103,
"Los Angeles-North Main Street", in downtown Los Angeles. A site is a
place; a monitor is one instrument at that place. This site runs five
instruments, and keeping the right one is part of the work.

You get one CSV per calendar year, because EPA's download tool splits
at the year boundary. Your window, December 2024 through February 2025,
straddles it. The files are byte for byte what the tool returned:
nothing was cleaned, sorted, or reformatted. `data/SOURCE.md` in your
starter repo records the source URL, the exact download selections, and
the file checksums, so you can re-download and compare.

## Reference checkpoints

This course discloses expected values on purpose: the CHECK blocks in
`hw1.R` and the answer table in `results_spec.md` print them. The
pipeline from raw file to answer is the assignment; the numbers were
never the secret.

Anchors you can check your work against:

- EPA's 24-hour PM2.5 standard is 35 µg/m³. One of your six numbers
  counts the days above it.
- The shipped file carries EPA's own Air Quality Index in the
  `Daily AQI Value` column. On the peak day it reads 182, a level EPA
  labels "Unhealthy".
- [Schollaert et al. (2025)](https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/acs.estlett.5c00486)
  report a 101.7 µg/m³ peak at this monitor, drawn from EPA's
  real-time feed. Your file is the quality-assured archive, and it says
  something close but not identical. `data/SOURCE.md` explains why both
  numbers are right.

## What to submit

Two files, due Thursday, September 3, 8:40 am:

- `hw1.R`: your edited script.
- `results.csv`: written by your script, in the exact format
  `results_spec.md` specifies.

Upload by browser: open your private repo in the course GitHub
organization, drag both files onto the repo page, and commit. Sign-up
instructions are on Canvas. No git client is needed; git arrives in
session 7.

Before you upload, restart R and source your script from scratch. It
must run top to bottom in a fresh session with no errors. The grader
runs it exactly that way.

## How this one is weighted

| Dimension | Points | The question it asks |
|-----------|-------:|----------------------|
| Reproduces | 15 | Does the script run, start to finish, in a fresh session? |
| Correct | 60 | Are the six numbers right, and does your script compute them? |
| Verified | 15 | Did you check your own work? |
| Craft | 10 | Can someone else read it? |

The question points inside `hw1.R` sum to 100 and scale by 0.6 into
Correct. A `results.csv` with the right numbers and a script that does
not compute them scores 0 on Correct. Editing a CHECK block so it
passes scores worse than leaving it failing honestly. The full HW1
rubric ships in your starter as `rubric.md`; the course-wide grading
scheme is in the [syllabus](../syllabus.qmd#homework).
